title: How many settings did you try?
objectives: Report how many parameter settings you tried and the spread of their results.
Compare the best setting with the expected best under no edge.

screens.title: Forty-eight tries at nothing
screens.prose: `make_bars(phi=0.0)` is the twin of our data with the momentum taken out: there is no edge to find. We try 48 settings on its research years: 8 lookbacks, 3 entry thresholds (0, 1%, 2%) and 2 directions (follow or fade), at 2.5 bp. These are the 48 research Sharpes.
screens.question: The best setting scores 0.77. What produced it?

options.text: Luck: it is the highest of 48 noisy numbers
A rule that suits this share
options.why: There is nothing in this share to suit: the twin was built with no edge.
The engine is the honest one from l13. The 0.77 needs no bug.

options.text: A small edge the generator left in by accident
options.why: With `phi=0.0` each day's return is independent of the last. Any pattern found is noise.

hints.text: What is the true Sharpe of every one of these settings?
Zero: the data has no edge.
Each research Sharpe is zero plus noise. The best of 48 noise draws is the largest noise draw.

feedback.correct: The best of many noisy numbers is biased up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Remember how the twin was made.

byKey.fit: You read a search result as a discovery. On this data every setting's true Sharpe is zero.

explain.text: Every setting has a true Sharpe of zero here, yet the best scores 0.77 and the median −0.05. Choosing the maximum picks the luckiest draw. This is the **multiple-testing problem**.

screens.title: How lucky is lucky?
screens.prose: Suppose the 48 settings were independent. A no-edge Sharpe over four years then has sd about $1/\sqrt{4} = 0.5$. Each run below is one search: 48 such Sharpes, scored by whether the best reaches 0.77.
screens.question: Run at least 1,000 searches. What share find a best of 0.77 or more?

widget.accept: Any value from 0.93 to 0.97. The exact share is $1 - \Phi(1.54)^{48} = 0.953$.
widget.label: Share of searches

hints.text: Press Run 1,000 and read the first bar.
The first bar is the share of searches whose best reached 0.77.
It settles near 0.95.

feedback.correct: Almost every pure-noise search does at least as well.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the height of the first bar after 1,000 runs.

byKey.one: That is the chance for a single setting, $1 - \Phi(1.54) = 0.062$. The search has 48 chances.

explain.text: About 95% of noise searches reach 0.77: our best is ordinary for a search of 48. Our 48 are correlated, so they behave like fewer tries. That is one reason our best sits below this independent case.

screens.title: The expected best
screens.prose: The best of $N$ independent standard normals has a known mean. For $N = 10$ it is 1.539 (computed exactly, by integration). A Sharpe with sd $\sigma$ scales that: $E[\max_N] = \sigma \times E[\max \text{ of } N \text{ standard normals}]$.
screens.question: With $\sigma = 0.5$, what is the expected best of 10 settings? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Scale the standard-normal value by $\sigma$.
$\sigma = 0.5$ here.

feedback.correct: Ten tries on noise expect a best near 0.77.

byKey.unscaled: That is in standard-normal units. Multiply by the Sharpe's sd, 0.5.

explain.text: Ten no-edge settings expect a best of 0.77, marked on the curve. A single setting expects 0. That gap is the bar a searched result must clear.

screens.title: One hundred tries
screens.prose: Now $N = 100$, where the best of 100 standard normals averages 2.508. A rough rule, $\sqrt{2 \ln N}$, gives 3.03; it is the large-$N$ limit and runs high for small $N$.
screens.question: With $\sigma = 0.5$, what is the expected best of 100? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Same scaling as before.
Use 2.508, not the rough rule.

feedback.correct: Ten times the tries, about 60% more luck.

byKey.rough: You used $\sqrt{2 \ln 100} = 3.03$. At $N = 100$ it overstates by about a fifth: use 2.508.

explain.text: Ten times the tries lift the bar from 0.77 to 1.25. The expected best grows slowly with $N$, roughly like $\sqrt{2 \ln N}$, but it never stops growing. Edge case: at $N = 1$ it is 0, and there is nothing to deflate.

screens.title: The real data against its twin
screens.prose: The same 48 settings on the real `make_bars()`, beside the twin. With 2,000 simulated searches, the best of 48 standard normals averages 2.24. We scale it by the sd of the trial Sharpes.
screens.question: What is the expected best under no edge for the real grid? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Use the real column's sd.
Multiply 2.24 by 0.451.

feedback.correct: The real grid's best does not clear it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale the expected best of 48 by the real grid's sd.

byKey.twin: That uses the twin's sd. Use the real column.
byKey.half: That uses the theoretical sd of 0.5. The spread of the trials themselves is 0.451.

explain.text: The real best, 0.72, is below the 1.01 that noise alone would give. It is also a fade rule, the opposite of the momentum we planted. The real edge is there, but too small for four years and 48 tries to show.

screens.title: Does research predict the held-out year?
screens.prose: Each dot is one of the twin's 48 settings: its research Sharpe across, its held-out Sharpe up. If research picked real skill, high dots would sit to the right.
screens.question: What does the fitted line say?

options.text: Research rank tells us nothing about the held-out year
The best research settings do best held out
options.why: Look at the slope: it is near zero, so high research scores do not carry over.

options.text: Pick the worst research setting instead
options.why: A slope near zero says no relation at all, not a reliable reversal.

options.text: The held-out year was too short to judge
options.why: Short years are noisy, but 48 points still show no trend.

hints.text: Read the slope of the line.
Its slope is close to zero.
The slope is 0.12: knowing a setting's research score does not help guess its held-out score.

feedback.correct: On noise, ranks do not carry over.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Judge by the slope of the fitted line.

explain.text: The slope is 0.12, close to zero: the research winner is no better than the rest when the year changes. On data with an edge the slope would be positive. That is the test a lucky search fails.

screens.title: Which N?
screens.prose: Before this grid, the notebook tried 72 other settings on the same research years. All were dropped. The results note says: "Best of 48 settings: research Sharpe 0.77."
screens.question: What is the honest $N$ for the deflation?

widget.accept: 120: every distinct setting run on these data, kept or dropped.
widget.label: $N$

hints.text: Which settings could have produced the best?
Any of them, dropped or kept.

feedback.correct: Every run on the data counts.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every setting tried on the research years.

byKey.grid: You counted only the final grid. The 72 dropped settings were tries too, and any could have won.
byKey.one: Reporting one setting does not make it one trial. Count the search.

explain.text: All 120 settings were chances to find a lucky best, so $N = 120$. The best of 120 standard normals averages 2.57, against 2.24 for 48. The trial log starts before the first run (fin-ml, the deflated Sharpe ratio).

screens.title: What to report
screens.prose:
What you computed: with $N$ settings whose Sharpes have sd $s$,
$$E[\max_N] \approx s \cdot E\Big[\max_{i \le N} Z_i\Big], \quad Z_i \sim N(0, 1).$$
A best below it is no evidence of skill. fin-ml's deflated Sharpe ratio turns the same gap into a probability. Report $N$, the best, the median, $s$ and $E[\max_N]$.
screens.question: A grid's 10 settings all trade identically, since no threshold ever binds. What is the effective $N$?

options.text: 1: they are one rule, so there is only one try

options.why: Ten runs of the same trades give the same number ten times. There is only one draw of luck.
There is no partial count here: identical rules are one trial.
Overcounting raises the bar for no reason. Count distinct behaviour.

feedback.correct: Correlated settings count for fewer than $N$; identical ones count once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many different results can the grid produce?

explain.text: Identical settings are one trial, so the effective $N$ is 1. Our 48 are partly alike, which is why their sd is 0.40, not 0.5. Counting them as 48 is the cautious, honest default.

screens.title: The grid in code
screens.prose: Record every setting, research and held-out, in one table. `split_holdout` and `net_sharpe` are defined. Return a DataFrame indexed by lookback, with columns `research` and `held_out`, rounded to 3 places.
screens.question: Complete `grid_results(bars, lookbacks, cost_bp)`.

widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests on BARS and TWIN: the whole table, one column, one lookback at zero cost and a cost of 10 bp. One checks the index keeps the order given. Values compared exactly after rounding to 3 places. The first run loads NumPy and pandas, which takes about 15 seconds; later runs are quick.

hints.text: Each row is two numbers from `net_sharpe`.
One on `research`, one on `held_out`, same lookback and cost.
`rows[L] = [net_sharpe(research, L, cost_bp), net_sharpe(held_out, L, cost_bp)]`.

feedback.correct: Every setting, both periods, one table.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Score each lookback on both frames with the same cost.

explain.text: A grid table with both columns lets a reader see the research winner fail held out. In a real study you fill the held-out column only once, at the end. Here we show it to make the lesson's point.

screens.title: Summarise the trials
screens.prose: The note reports the whole search, not just the winner. Return a dict with `n`, `best`, `median` and `sd`, the sample sd with `ddof = 1`. Round all but `n` to 4 places; `n` is a plain `int`.
screens.question: Complete `trial_summary(sharpes)`.

widget.starter:
import pandas as pd

def trial_summary(sharpes):
    s = pd.Series(sharpes, dtype=float)
    return {"n": ..., "best": ..., "median": ..., "sd": ...}   # sd with ddof = 1, round to 4
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests on hand lists: an even and an odd count, all equal values, all negative values, a tuple, and the type of n. Dicts compared exactly. The first run loads pandas, which takes about 15 seconds.

hints.text: pandas has `max`, `median` and `std`.
`std(ddof=1)` is the sample sd.
Wrap each in `round(float(...), 4)` and `n` in `int(len(s))`.

feedback.correct: The search, summarised in four numbers.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check `ddof = 1` and the rounding.

explain.text: The median shows what a typical setting does; the best shows what the search found. With all-equal trials the sd is 0, the sign that the grid was really one setting.

screens.title: The bar in code
screens.prose: Simulate the bar. Each row of `draws` is one search of `n` no-edge settings; the mean of the row maxima, times `sd`, is the expected best. Round it to 3 places. Edge case: one setting has no search, so return 0.0. `deflated_verdict` is True when `best` beats that bar.
screens.question: Complete `expected_max_sharpe` and `deflated_verdict`.

widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests: expected bests for 1 to 100 settings, another seed, and six verdicts, including both grids and one setting. Numbers compared exactly after rounding to 3 places; the draws must be one `(sims, n)` array from the given generator. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: `draws.max(axis=1)` is the best of each search.
Average those maxima, multiply by `sd`, round to 3.
`round(float(draws.max(axis=1).mean() * sd), 3)`; the verdict is `best > expected_max_sharpe(n, sd)`.

feedback.correct: The bar, and the verdict against it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the maximum across each row, then the mean down the rows.

explain.text: The twin's best, 0.77, falls short of 0.889, and the real grid's 0.72 short of 1.011. The 8-lookback grid's 0.547 clears its own bar of 0.489. But it was one corner of the 48, so the 48 is the honest $N$.

screens.title: The line in the note
screens.prose: Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016) counted hundreds of published factors. They argued a new one needs a t statistic near 3, not 2. Our study's results note needs one line on trials.
screens.question: Which line belongs in the results note?

options.text: 48 settings tried; best research Sharpe 0.72; expected best under no edge 1.01

options.why: That hides the search. Without $N$ a reader cannot tell 0.55 from luck.

options.text: Best of 8 lookbacks: 0.55, above the no-edge bar of 0.49
options.why: The 8 were one corner of a 48-setting search on the same data. Reporting the corner sets the bar too low.

options.text: No line needed: the held-out year settles it
options.why: One held-out year has a standard error near 1. The trial count tells the reader how far to trust research.

hints.text: A reader needs $N$, the best and the bar.
The bar uses all 48 settings.
Choose the line that states 48, the best and the expected best.

feedback.correct: Three numbers let any reader do the check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose the line that lets a reader judge the search.

explain.text: Stating $N$, the best and the bar lets a reader check the claim in seconds. It is the same discipline Harvey, Liu and Zhu ask of factor research. A desk reads that line before the Sharpe.

ideas: The best of $N$ noisy Sharpes is biased up: on data with no edge, 48 settings found a best of 0.77.
The expected best under no edge is the sd of the trials times the mean best of $N$ standard normals.
Report $N$ (every setting tried, dropped ones too), the best, the median, the spread and the expected best.

formula.name: Expected best under no edge
formula.note: $E[\max Z]$: 0 for $N = 1$, 1.54 for 10, 2.23 for 48 (2.24 in the 2,000 simulated searches), 2.51 for 100.

summary.trap: Reporting the best setting without $N$, or counting only the final grid.

quiz.prose: Edge case. A pension fund fixed one rule in advance and ran nothing else.
quiz.question: What is the expected best Sharpe under no edge for its search?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What is the mean of one draw of noise?

byKey.half: 0.5 is the sd of one setting's Sharpe, not its expected value.

explain.text: With $N = 1$ the expected best is the mean of one no-edge Sharpe, 0. Its Sharpe still has a standard error, but there is no selection to correct.

quiz.prose: A search tries 100 settings whose Sharpes have sd 0.3. The best of 100 standard normals averages 2.508.
quiz.question: What is the expected best under no edge? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale 2.508 by the sd.

quiz.prose: A note says: "Lookback 2 has research Sharpe 0.55." Nothing else about the search.
quiz.question: What is missing for a reader to judge it?

options.text: How many settings were tried, and their median, spread and expected best
More decimal places on the Sharpe, to show its precision
options.why: Precision is not the problem. The search behind the number is.

options.text: A chart of the equity curve over the research years
options.why: A chart shows the same research result. It cannot reveal how many others were tried.

feedback.correct: The search, not just the winner.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What would change how much 0.55 means?

explain.text: The same 0.55 is strong as one try and weak as the best of 48. Only $N$ and the spread of the trials tell the reader which.

quiz.prose: A grid has 40 settings, but the 10 thresholds never bind, so the 40 runs are really 4 distinct rules.
quiz.question: Which $N$ should the deflation use?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count distinct behaviour.

byKey.all: Identical runs give the same number. They are one draw of luck each, not ten.
byKey.ten: That counts the thresholds, which change nothing here.

explain.text: Each distinct rule is one chance to be lucky, so $N = 4$. Partly alike settings count for somewhere between.
